figures.name: Ignatius of Antioch
figures.summary: Ignatius led the church in Antioch, one of the great cities of the early Christian world. Late in life he was arrested and marched across the empire to Rome to be killed by wild animals in the arena. On that long journey he wrote letters to churches along the way, and in them he begged his friends not to rescue him, because he wanted his death to bear witness to the Jesus he loved. His seven surviving letters press two things hard: that Jesus truly came in the flesh and truly suffered, against teachers who said his body only seemed real, and that the scattered churches should hold together around their bishop and the one table. Writing to the church at Smyrna, he is the first writer we know of to speak of the catholic church, meaning the whole church rather than a single congregation.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His letters are among the earliest Christian writings we have outside the New Testament, and they show a man facing death with steadiness rather than bravado.

figures.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
figures.place: Smyrna in Asia Minor, modern Turkey
figures.summary: Polycarp was a bridge between the apostles and the next generations, said to have known the apostle John personally. As an old man he was arrested during a local persecution and ordered to curse Christ to save his life. He answered that he had served Christ for many years and had received only good from him, so he could not turn on his King now. His own letter to the church at Philippi survives, woven through with lines from Paul and the other apostolic writings, which shows those writings were already being read as authority. The account of his martyrdom, written by his church soon afterward, is the oldest surviving story of a Christian martyr outside the New Testament, and his people gathered his bones and kept the day of his death, the beginning of the church's habit of remembering its martyrs.
figures.whyTheyMatter: The account of his death is one of the oldest and most moving martyr stories the church preserved, and it shaped how Christians thought about faithfulness under pressure.

figures.name: Justin Martyr
figures.place: Born in Samaria, taught in Rome
figures.summary: Justin spent his early years searching through the philosophies of his day before he met an old man by the sea who pointed him to the Hebrew prophets and to Christ. He kept wearing the philosopher's cloak after his conversion, because he believed Christianity was the truth all the great thinkers had been reaching toward. He opened a school in Rome and wrote careful defenses of the faith addressed to the emperor himself, and he was eventually beheaded for refusing to sacrifice to the Roman gods.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He was one of the first to argue that faith and serious thinking belong together, a claim that still steadies believers who are told they must choose between the two.

figures.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
figures.summary: Irenaeus grew up in Smyrna where he heard Polycarp teach, then served as a pastor in the rough frontier city of Lyon. He spent his energy answering teachers who claimed secret knowledge and a hidden gospel, insisting instead that the real message of Jesus was public, handed down openly from the apostles, and held in common by churches everywhere. He wrote that the glory of God is a human being fully alive. His great work, usually called Against Heresies and written around 180, argued that the true faith was the one taught openly by bishops who could trace their succession to the apostles, and that the church had four Gospels, no more and no fewer. His own theology turned on a word he took from Paul, recapitulation: Christ lived through every stage of the human story Adam had ruined and set it right from the inside.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He helped the church see that the gospel is not a secret for insiders but a public truth anyone can receive.

figures.name: Perpetua
figures.summary: Perpetua was a young, educated mother with a nursing infant when she was arrested for being a Christian during a wave of persecution. Part of her prison account survives in her own words, which makes it one of the earliest writings we have by a Christian woman. Her father pleaded with her again and again to renounce her faith and live, and her refusal, recorded plainly and without drama, still reads as one of the most human documents of the early church. She died in the arena at Carthage on 7 March 203 beside Felicity, an enslaved woman who had given birth in prison days before the games. The account that preserves them sets the noblewoman and the slave side by side in death, and the church has named them together ever since.
figures.whyTheyMatter: Her diary lets a reader hear an ordinary believer speak across eighteen centuries, frightened and resolute at the same time.

figures.name: Tertullian
figures.summary: Tertullian was a sharp-tongued Latin writer who became one of the first major Christian voices in the language of the Western church. He coined words and phrases the church still uses to talk about God as three in one. He was brilliant and combative, and in his later years he drifted toward a strict, fringe movement that the wider church did not follow, which is a reminder that gifted people can still lose their way. Around 213, in a treatise against a teacher named Praxeas, he described God as one substance in three persons, the formula the Latin church kept. It was also Tertullian who told Rome that its executions only multiplied the Christians, because the blood of the martyrs worked like seed.
figures.whyTheyMatter: Much of the vocabulary Western Christians use for the Trinity traces back to his restless, demanding mind.

figures.name: Origen of Alexandria
figures.summary: Origen was perhaps the most learned man of the early church, a tireless student of Scripture who produced commentaries, sermons, and a massive side-by-side comparison of biblical texts. He gave his whole life to teaching and lived with severe self-denial, and he was tortured during a persecution late in life and died of his injuries. Some of his more speculative ideas were later judged to have gone too far, yet his devotion to understanding the Bible was never in doubt. That comparison, the Hexapla, set six versions of the Old Testament in parallel columns, and his On First Principles was the first attempt to lay out Christian teaching as a whole. He read Scripture in layers, a plain sense with a spiritual sense beneath it, and that way of reading shaped Christian interpretation for a thousand years. Three centuries after his death, some of his speculations, such as the existence of souls before their bodies, were formally condemned.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He set an example of pouring a whole life into the study of Scripture, and the church learned from both his strengths and his overreach.

figures.name: Antony of Egypt
figures.place: The Egyptian desert east of the Nile
figures.summary: Antony was the son of Christian farmers in Egypt, orphaned as a young man, who heard the Gospel read in church where Jesus tells a rich man to sell everything and give to the poor, and took it as spoken to him. He gave away his land, apprenticed himself to an old hermit, and moved deeper and deeper into the desert, where he fought what he described as a long war with temptation and despair. Others came to learn from him, and loose colonies of monks grew up around his cell. He left the desert twice for Alexandria, once to encourage Christians during persecution and once to support Athanasius against the Arians. Athanasius wrote his Life soon after his death, and the book spread across the empire; Augustine heard the story of Antony shortly before his own conversion.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He gave the church the monastic protest, the conviction that when the faith becomes comfortable and respectable, someone must go into the desert to remember what it costs.

figures.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
figures.role: Bishop and defender of the faith
figures.summary: Athanasius was a young deacon at the Council of Nicaea in 325, where the church confronted a teaching that Jesus was a created being and not truly God. For the rest of his life he defended the conviction that the Son is fully divine, and he paid for it by being driven into exile five separate times. The struggle was so lopsided at points that people spoke of Athanasius against the world. In On the Incarnation he argued that only God himself could restore the image of God in fallen humanity, so a Savior who was less than God could not save. His Life of Antony carried the story of the desert monks across the empire, and his Easter letter of 367 is the first surviving list of exactly the twenty seven books of the New Testament.
figures.whyTheyMatter: Much of what Christians confess about Jesus being truly God owes a debt to a man who would not back down even when nearly everyone in power was against him.

figures.name: Ephrem the Syrian
figures.place: Nisibis, then Edessa, in upper Mesopotamia
figures.summary: Ephrem served the church at Nisibis on the frontier between Rome and Persia as a teacher and deacon, and when the city was handed over to Persia in 363 he moved west to Edessa with other Christian refugees. He wrote in Syriac, not Greek or Latin, and he did his theology in hymns, hundreds of them, which he set for choirs, including choirs of women, to sing in church. His poetry treats the mysteries of God with reverence and warns against those who pry into God as if he were a problem to be solved. Near the end of his life, during a famine in Edessa, he organized relief for the starving. The Syriac churches call him the Harp of the Spirit, and in 1920 the Catholic Church named him a Doctor of the Church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He is a reminder that the early church was not only Greek and Latin, and that some of its deepest theology was sung rather than argued.

figures.name: Macrina the Younger
figures.summary: Macrina was the eldest child of the remarkable family that produced Basil the Great and Gregory of Nyssa. When the young man she was promised to died before the wedding, she refused all other matches and turned the family estate into a community of prayer, persuading her mother to live alongside their former servants as equals. By her brother Gregory's account, it was Macrina who drew Basil away from pride in his education and toward a life given to God. Gregory wrote her Life after her death, and in his dialogue On the Soul and the Resurrection he cast her as his teacher, reasoning with him about death and the life to come as she lay dying.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She was the teacher of the teachers, and her story shows that some of the church's great theology was learned first at the feet of a woman who held no office.

figures.name: Frumentius and King Ezana
figures.place: Aksum, in modern Ethiopia and Eritrea
figures.summary: Frumentius was a young Christian from Tyre whose ship was attacked at a Red Sea port, and he was carried to the royal court of Aksum, where he rose to become a trusted adviser. He encouraged Christian merchants to gather for worship, then traveled to Alexandria and asked Athanasius to send a bishop; Athanasius consecrated Frumentius himself and sent him back. King Ezana embraced the faith, and his coins, which had carried the pagan crescent and disc, began to bear the cross. When the Arian emperor Constantius later wrote to Ezana demanding that Frumentius be sent to Alexandria to be examined by an Arian bishop, Athanasius preserved the emperor's letter in one of his own writings. Ethiopian Christians remember Frumentius as Abba Salama, father of peace.
figures.whyTheyMatter: They stand at the head of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, one of the oldest continuous churches in the world, which means Christianity in Africa is older than Christianity in most of Europe.

figures.name: Basil the Great
figures.summary: Basil came from a remarkable family in central Turkey and gave up a promising career to serve the church. As a bishop he built one of the first large complexes to care for the sick and the poor, a kind of early hospital, and he wrote rules for monastic life that still guide communities today. His treatise On the Holy Spirit, written around 375, defended worshiping the Spirit together with the Father and the Son, and it prepared the ground for the Council of Constantinople in 381, which he did not live to see. He preached that the bread hoarded in the rich man's storehouse belonged to the hungry, and the hospital outside Caesarea, which people called the Basileias, was that sermon made of brick. He is counted with his brother Gregory of Nyssa and his friend Gregory of Nazianzus as the Cappadocian Fathers, and it was his elder sister Macrina, whom his own writings never mention, who by Gregory's account first turned him toward the monastic life.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He showed that deep theology and practical care for the poor are not rivals but partners.

figures.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
figures.summary: Gregory was a thoughtful, sometimes reluctant churchman who preferred quiet study to public office. Pressed into leadership of the small Nicene congregation in Constantinople, he preached five sermons there in 380, the Theological Orations, defending the full deity of the Son and the Spirit so clearly that the Orthodox church calls him simply the Theologian. He argued that whatever part of human nature Christ did not take on, he did not heal, a principle that still anchors the confession that Jesus was fully human, mind included. He presided for a time over the Council of Constantinople in 381, found the quarreling unbearable, and resigned, retreating to write poetry about his own struggles.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His careful words about the Trinity helped the wider church settle what it believes, and his honesty about his own weariness makes him easy to recognize.

figures.name: Gregory of Nyssa
figures.summary: The younger brother of Basil, Gregory of Nyssa was the most original mind of the three Cappadocians. In his Life of Moses he read the climb up Sinai as a picture of the soul always stretching forward into God, a growth that never ends because God has no limit. He wrote the Life of his older sister Macrina and a dialogue on the resurrection in which she is his teacher, grieving and hoping at her deathbed. In a sermon on Ecclesiastes he asked by what right anyone could put a price on a human being made in the image of God, one of the very few ancient voices to condemn slavery itself rather than only its cruelties.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He gave the church some of its richest reflection on the endless depth of God and on growing closer to him over a lifetime.

figures.name: Ambrose of Milan
figures.summary: Ambrose was a Roman governor, not even baptized, when the people of Milan suddenly acclaimed him their bishop. He grew into the role with seriousness, preaching, writing hymns, and standing up to emperors. On one famous occasion he refused to give communion to the emperor Theodosius until he repented for ordering a massacre, insisting that no ruler stands above the moral law. He was elected in 374 while still preparing for baptism, and he was baptized and consecrated within about a week. His hymns taught the people Nicene faith by giving them something to sing, and at Easter in 387 he baptized Augustine.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He set a lasting example that earthly power must answer to God, and his preaching helped lead Augustine to faith.

figures.name: John Chrysostom
figures.summary: John was such a gifted speaker that later generations gave him the nickname Chrysostom, meaning golden-mouthed. He preached plainly and pointedly, urging the rich to care for the poor and calling the powerful to account, which made him beloved by ordinary people and dangerous to the court. He was twice sent into exile and died worn out on the road. His hundreds of surviving sermons on Matthew, John, and the letters of Paul are still read as models of preaching that stays close to the text. As archbishop of Constantinople he cut the luxuries of his own household and clashed with the empress Eudoxia, which led to his exile. The liturgy that bears his name is still the ordinary Sunday service of the Orthodox church. His sermons also include harsh attacks on the Jews that later Christians used as a weapon, and honest readers name them.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His sermons remain a model of preaching that refuses to flatter the powerful and keeps returning to the needs of the poor.

figures.name: Jerome
figures.place: Born in Dalmatia, settled in Bethlehem
figures.summary: Jerome was a brilliant and famously prickly scholar who learned Hebrew and Greek so he could translate the Bible into the everyday Latin of his time. The result, later called the Vulgate, became the standard Bible of the Western church for more than a thousand years. He was quick to argue and slow to forgive, a difficult man who nonetheless gave the church a gift it used for centuries. In Bethlehem he worked alongside Paula, a Roman noblewoman, and her daughter Eustochium, who funded his monasteries, studied Hebrew with him, and pressed him to keep translating. He insisted on going back to the Hebrew rather than relying only on the Greek translation of the Old Testament, a choice that worried even Augustine.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His translation put the Scriptures into the common language of the West for a millennium and set a high standard for working from the original texts.

figures.name: Augustine of Hippo
figures.place: Hippo in North Africa, modern Algeria
figures.summary: Augustine spent his youth chasing ambition, pleasure, and a string of philosophies, all while his mother prayed for him. After a long inner struggle he came to faith in Milan, became a bishop in his North African hometown, and wrote with rare honesty about his own restless heart. His Confessions reads like a man talking to God about everything he got wrong, and his other writings shaped Western Christianity more than almost any figure outside the New Testament. The book, written in the late 390s, opens by telling God that the human heart is restless until it rests in him. After Rome was sacked in 410 he wrote The City of God, arguing that two loves make two cities, one built on the love of self and one on the love of God. Against Pelagius he argued that human beings cannot save themselves by effort and that grace always comes first. He died in 430 while the Vandals besieged his city.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He gave the church language for grace, sin, and the restless heart, and his story assures every latecomer that no past is too tangled for God.

figures.name: Patrick
figures.summary: Patrick was the son of a Christian family in Roman Britain who was seized by Irish raiders at sixteen and spent six years as a slave herding animals, where, by his own account, he began to pray. He escaped, went home, and later returned to the land of his captivity as a bishop. Two of his writings survive, his Confession and a letter condemning a British Christian warlord whose men had killed and enslaved newly baptized converts. Much of the later legend about him is legend, but those two short texts show a humble, unlearned man who felt himself a stranger in Ireland and stayed anyway.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He went back to the people who had enslaved him, and he wrote one of the earliest Christian protests against Christians trafficking in human beings.

figures.name: Benedict of Nursia
figures.summary: Benedict left the chaos of a collapsing Roman world to live as a hermit, then gathered followers and wrote a short, sane guidebook for life in community. His Rule balanced prayer, work, study, and rest, and asked for moderation rather than heroic extremes. Communities across Europe adopted it, and for centuries monasteries became places where learning, farming, and worship were kept alive. Most of what we know of his life comes from a book of stories written by Gregory the Great decades later. His Rule, some seventy three short chapters, opens with the word listen, and it asks monks to promise stability, faithfulness to the monastic way of life, and obedience. It makes room for the weak, the old, and the young, and it tells the abbot to seek to be loved rather than feared.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His simple pattern of prayer and work preserved learning through Europe's hardest centuries and still guides Christians seeking a steady rhythm of life.

figures.name: Gregory the Great
figures.summary: Gregory came from a wealthy Roman family and gave away his inheritance to become a monk, only to be pulled into leadership as bishop of Rome during plague, famine, and political collapse. He organized relief for the hungry, sent missionaries to England, and wrote a practical handbook on caring for souls that pastors used for centuries. He called himself the servant of the servants of God, a title later popes kept. His Book of Pastoral Rule, written as he took office, warned that the same word does not suit every hearer, so the proud and the timid, the rich and the poor, must each be addressed differently. When his missionaries reached England, he advised them to destroy the idols of the English but not their temples, which were to be cleansed and turned into churches.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He combined deep humility with steady administration, and his writing on pastoral care still speaks to anyone responsible for others.

figures.name: Maximus the Confessor
figures.summary: By the most common tradition, Maximus served at the imperial court before leaving it to become a monk. When the emperors promoted the teaching that Christ had only one will, a compromise meant to reunite the divided churches, Maximus refused it, arguing that a Christ without a human will had not fully become human and so could not fully save us. He was arrested, tried in Constantinople, and when he would not yield, his tongue and his right hand were cut off so he could neither speak nor write. He died in exile on the eastern shore of the Black Sea. Less than twenty years later the Third Council of Constantinople affirmed exactly what he had suffered for.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His teaching that God became human so that humans might share in the life of God shapes Orthodox theology to this day, and his refusal shows that small words about Christ can be worth a life.

figures.name: John of Damascus
figures.place: Damascus, then the monastery of Mar Saba near Jerusalem
figures.summary: John came from a Christian family that served in the government of the Muslim caliphs at Damascus, and by tradition he held a post there himself before becoming a monk near Jerusalem. When the Byzantine emperor began destroying icons, John, living under Muslim rule and beyond the emperor's reach, wrote three treatises defending them. His argument was that the invisible God had made himself visible in Jesus, so picturing Christ confesses the incarnation rather than denying it, and that honoring matter is fitting because God worked salvation through matter. His Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith gathered the teaching of the Greek fathers into one ordered work, and he was one of the first Christian writers to describe and answer Islam. Some of his hymns are still sung at Easter.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He shows the church thinking clearly as a minority under another religion's rule, and his defense of icons is at bottom a defense of the incarnation.

figures.name: Cyril and Methodius
figures.dates: Cyril around 827 to 869; Methodius around 815 to 885
figures.summary: Cyril and Methodius were brothers from Thessalonica who had grown up hearing the Slavic language spoken around them. In 863 the Byzantine emperor sent them to Moravia at the request of its ruler, who wanted teachers who could speak to his people in their own tongue. They created an alphabet for the Slavic language and translated the liturgy and the Scriptures into it. German clergy objected that only Hebrew, Greek, and Latin were fit for worship, and the brothers went to Rome, where the pope approved the Slavonic liturgy. Cyril died there in 869. Methodius went back as archbishop, was imprisoned for more than two years by rival bishops, and kept working until his death. Their disciples carried the work into Bulgaria, where the Cyrillic alphabet named for Cyril took shape.
figures.whyTheyMatter: They insisted that every people should worship God in its own language, and much of the Slavic world still reads its Bible in letters that descend from their work.

figures.name: Anselm of Canterbury
figures.place: Born in Italy, archbishop in England
figures.summary: Anselm was a gentle monk and teacher at the abbey of Bec in Normandy who rose to become archbishop of Canterbury, a post that brought him into repeated conflict with English kings over the freedom of the church, and twice into exile. He described his work as faith seeking understanding, meaning that he believed first and then tried to grasp what he believed. In the Proslogion, written as a prayer, he framed his argument that God is that than which nothing greater can be thought, an argument philosophers still debate. In Why God Became Man, finished in 1098, he argued that sin had dishonored God beyond any human power to repay, so only one who was both God and man could make satisfaction.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He showed that prayer and rigorous thinking can live in the same person, and his question of why God became man still anchors how many Christians understand the cross.

figures.name: Bernard of Clairvaux
figures.summary: Bernard joined a struggling new monastery as a young man and soon founded his own at Clairvaux, which grew into a center of reform. He was an electrifying preacher whose words could move kings and crowds, and his writing about the love of God, in On Loving God and in eighty six sermons on the Song of Songs, is tender even now. He also threw himself into the politics of his age, and in 1146 his preaching raised the Second Crusade, which ended in disaster. In the same years he rode to the Rhineland to silence a monk whose preaching was stirring mobs to kill Jews. He was a child of his time and, at moments, a rebuke to it.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His writings on loving God shaped centuries of Christian devotion, and his life shows both the beauty and the blind spots of a passionate believer.

figures.name: Hildegard of Bingen
figures.summary: Hildegard was given to the religious life as a child and grew up enclosed with an older nun at the monastery of Disibodenberg, later becoming leader of its women. At forty two she received what she described as a divine command to write down the visions she had carried since childhood, and Scivias, her first great book, took ten years. She went on to compose music still performed today, write on medicine and the natural world, found her own convent at Rupertsberg, and correspond with popes, an emperor, and Bernard of Clairvaux. In her sixties she made preaching tours along the Rhine, rebuking the clergy for corruption. Near the end of her life her convent was placed under interdict because she had buried a man the authorities considered excommunicate, and she refused to dig him up, insisting he had been reconciled to the church. The interdict was lifted months before she died. In 2012 she was named a Doctor of the Church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She used every gift she had, in music, medicine, and theology, in an age that gave women little room, and she told the powerful the truth.

figures.name: Francis of Assisi
figures.summary: Francis was the son of a wealthy cloth merchant who lived for parties and dreams of knightly glory until a series of encounters with the poor and with Christ turned him around. He gave up everything, even the clothes off his back, and began a life of poverty, preaching, and care for lepers and outcasts. The simple brotherhood he started spread across Europe, and his joy in creation and his gentleness drew people who had given up on the church. In 1219, in the middle of the Fifth Crusade, he crossed the battle lines in Egypt to preach to the sultan al-Kamil, who received him courteously and sent him back unharmed. Near the end of his life, nearly blind and in pain, he wrote the Canticle of the Creatures, praising God for brother sun and sister moon, and even for sister death.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He reminded a comfortable church that following Jesus can mean traveling light, and his love for the poor and for creation still pulls at people far beyond the faith.

figures.name: Thomas Aquinas
figures.summary: Thomas came from a noble family who locked him up to stop him from joining the new order of preaching friars, but he joined anyway. A large, quiet man whom classmates nicknamed the dumb ox, he became the most systematic thinker of the Middle Ages, working to show that reason and faith point to the same God. Near the end of his life he had an experience in prayer after which he said all he had written seemed like straw, and he set down his pen. His Summa Theologiae, written as a guide for beginners, is built of questions, and in each one he states the strongest objections to his own view before he answers them. He left it unfinished.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His patient effort to hold together careful reasoning and deep faith still shapes how many Christians think, and his final humility keeps that achievement in proportion.

figures.name: Gregory Palamas
figures.summary: Gregory was a monk of Mount Athos who defended the hesychasts, monks who prayed the Jesus Prayer in stillness and claimed to see the uncreated light that shone from Christ at the Transfiguration. A learned critic named Barlaam of Calabria mocked them, arguing that God could be known only indirectly. Gregory answered that God's essence is utterly beyond us, but God truly gives himself to us in his energies, so the one who prays can genuinely share in God's life without becoming God. Councils in Constantinople upheld him, and he became archbishop of Thessalonica, where he was once captured and held for a year by the Turks. The Orthodox church remembers him on the second Sunday of Lent.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He defended the conviction that prayer is real communion with God and not only thinking about him, and his distinction still shapes how the Orthodox understand salvation.

figures.name: Sergius of Radonezh
figures.summary: Sergius went into the forest as a young man with his brother and built a small wooden church dedicated to the Holy Trinity. Followers gathered, and the hermitage grew into the Trinity monastery, which became the spiritual heart of Russia. He did the manual work of the community himself, dressed in patched clothes, and refused to become metropolitan of Moscow when it was offered to him. Tradition says he blessed Prince Dmitry before the battle of Kulikovo in 1380. His disciples founded dozens of monasteries across the northern forests, and Andrei Rublev's icon of the Trinity was painted for the monastery he founded.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He is the father of Russian monasticism, and his humility became the Russian church's picture of holiness.

figures.name: John Wycliffe
figures.summary: Wycliffe was an Oxford scholar who grew convinced that ordinary people should be able to read the Bible in their own language and that the church of his day had drifted from its source. He pushed for an English Bible and criticized the wealth and corruption of church leaders. His followers, called Lollards, carried hand copied English Scriptures and his teaching into the countryside, and his books reached Prague, where they shaped Jan Hus. He died of natural causes, but the Council of Constance condemned him in 1415, and in 1428 his remains were dug up, burned, and the ashes thrown into the river Swift.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He was an early voice for putting the Bible in the hands of common people, and the movement he sparked helped prepare the ground for later reform.

figures.name: Julian of Norwich
figures.summary: In May 1373, when she was thirty and so ill she was given the last rites, Julian received a series of sixteen visions, which she called showings, of the suffering of Christ and the love of God. She recovered and spent the next twenty years and more thinking about what she had seen, writing first a short account and then a much longer one. Revelations of Divine Love is the earliest surviving book in English known to have been written by a woman. She lived as an anchoress, walled into a cell attached to the church of St. Julian in Norwich, in a city that had lived through plague and revolt, and people came to her window for counsel. She wrote of God's love with a daring tenderness, spoke of Christ as our mother, and heard the promise that all shall be well without pretending she understood how.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She held together the reality of sin and suffering and an unshakable trust in the love of God, and she refused to let either cancel the other.

figures.name: Catherine of Siena
figures.summary: Catherine was one of the youngest of the many children of a dyer in Siena. She refused the marriage her family planned, joined a lay order of Dominican women, and lived for years in near silence and prayer in a small room in her parents' house before turning outward to nurse the sick and visit prisoners. Without any office she became a voice the powerful could not ignore, dictating hundreds of letters to popes, kings, and city governments, calling them to peace and to reform. In 1376 she went to Avignon and urged Pope Gregory the Eleventh to return the papacy to Rome, and he entered Rome in January 1377. Her Dialogue records her conversation with God. She died in Rome at thirty three, worn out by fasting and grief over the divided church, and in 1970 she became one of the first two women named Doctors of the Church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: A young woman with no rank told popes what they needed to hear, and she did it out of love for the church, not contempt for it.

figures.name: Jan Hus
figures.place: Prague in Bohemia, modern Czech Republic
figures.summary: Hus was a popular preacher in Prague who took up many of Wycliffe's concerns, calling the church back to Scripture and against corruption. Promised safe passage to defend his views at a great council, he went, and the promise was broken. He was condemned and burned at the stake, reportedly singing as the fire was lit. The burning took place at Constance on 6 July 1415. The Czech church that grew from his memory gave the cup to lay people at communion, and the Moravian Brethren who later sent missionaries around the world traced their roots to that church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His courage and his betrayal were remembered for a century, and Martin Luther later saw himself as walking the road Hus had opened.

figures.name: Martin Luther
figures.summary: Luther was a German monk tormented by the question of how a sinful person could ever stand before a holy God, until he found his answer in the Bible's promise that we are made right with God by trust in Christ, not by our own efforts. In 1517 he posted a list of objections to the selling of forgiveness, and the argument that followed split Western Christianity. He translated the Bible into vivid German, married a former nun, and wrote with a force that could be both deeply pastoral and harshly cruel, especially in his ugly words about Jews late in life.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He recovered the assurance that God accepts us by grace through faith, a discovery that still sets anxious consciences free, even as his worst writings stand as a warning.

figures.name: Katharina von Bora
figures.role: Former nun and manager of the Luther household
figures.summary: Katharina was placed in a convent as a young girl. In 1523, after reading the reformers' writings, she and several other nuns escaped hidden in a merchant's wagon and were brought to Wittenberg, where Luther tried to find them husbands. She married Luther himself in June 1525. She turned the former monastery where they lived into a working household of farm, brewery, garden, and boarding house for students, and managed the family's money, which Luther could not. They had six children and lost two. Luther called her his lord Katie and trusted her judgment. After his death in 1546 she lost much of their property to war and plague and died in 1552 after a cart accident while fleeing plague.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She showed that the Reformation's recovery of ordinary vocation was lived first in kitchens and fields, and much of Luther's work rested on hers.

figures.name: William Tyndale
figures.summary: Tyndale was an English scholar consumed by the goal of putting the Bible into plain English, said to have told a learned man that he would make a plowboy know Scripture better than the clergy did. Forbidden to do the work at home, he fled to the continent, translated the New Testament, and had it smuggled into England in bales of cloth. He was finally betrayed, strangled, and burned, praying with his last breath that the king of England would have his eyes opened.
figures.whyTheyMatter: So much of the English Bible still echoes his phrasing that millions read his words without knowing his name.

figures.name: Thomas Cranmer
figures.summary: Cranmer was a cautious scholar who became archbishop of Canterbury under King Henry the Eighth and helped steer England's break with Rome. His great gift was language, and he shaped the prayers and services of the Book of Common Prayer, whose cadences are still used and quoted today. Under a later Catholic queen he was condemned, and after first signing recantations out of fear he recanted those too, thrusting into the fire first the hand that had signed them.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His prayers gave English-speaking Christians words for worship, marriage, and death that have lasted nearly five centuries, and his final hours show both human fear and hard-won courage.

figures.name: Bartolomé de las Casas
figures.role: Friar, bishop, and defender of Indigenous peoples
figures.summary: Las Casas went to the Caribbean as a young colonist and held land and native laborers like the other Spaniards. Preparing a sermon in 1514, he read a passage in the book of Sirach about offering sacrifices from what was taken from the poor, and he gave up his holdings and began preaching against the system he had profited from. He became a Dominican friar and spent the next fifty years arguing before kings and councils that the native peoples were fully human and could not be enslaved or converted by force. His Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies documented atrocities in detail. Early on he had suggested bringing enslaved Africans to spare the native peoples, and in his later History of the Indies he said he had come to regret that advice deeply.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He stood inside the conquest, saw his own sin, and spent his life turning against it, including the part of it he had once recommended.

figures.name: The Anabaptists
figures.summary: The Anabaptists were believers who concluded that baptism should follow a personal, adult decision to follow Christ, so they baptized one another again, which gave them their name. They generally refused to take up the sword or to mix the church with the power of the state, convictions that made them hunted by Catholic and Protestant rulers alike. Many were drowned, burned, or driven from their homes, yet the movement survived in groups such as the Mennonites and later the Amish. Their convictions were first set down at Schleitheim in 1527. A former Dutch priest named Menno Simons joined them in 1536 and gathered the scattered and persecuted communities, which is why many of their descendants are still called Mennonites.
figures.whyTheyMatter: They insisted that faith cannot be forced and that following Jesus may mean refusing violence, ideas the wider church took centuries to take seriously.

figures.name: Ignatius of Loyola
figures.role: Soldier and founder of the Jesuits
figures.summary: Ignatius was a Basque nobleman and soldier whose leg was shattered by a cannonball at Pamplona in 1521. During a long recovery, with nothing to read but a life of Christ and stories of the saints, he noticed that daydreams of glory left him empty while thoughts of following Christ left him at peace, and he began to pay attention to what that difference meant. From that attention came his Spiritual Exercises, a month long pattern of prayer and discernment still used by Catholics and Protestants. At the University of Paris he gathered a small group of companions, including Francis Xavier, and in 1540 the pope approved them as the Society of Jesus. The Jesuits became teachers, missionaries, and the sharpest instrument of Catholic renewal.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He taught Christians to notice how God moves in their desires, and his method of discernment is still one of the most practical guides to prayer ever written.

figures.name: John Calvin
figures.summary: Calvin was a quiet French scholar who meant to live a life of study until he was pressed into leading the reform of Geneva. He organized the church and the city with great care and wrote a clear, ordered summary of Christian teaching that has been read ever since. He was disciplined and at times severe, and his record includes the trial and execution of a man for heresy, a stain that honest readers do not hide. His Institutes of the Christian Religion first appeared in 1536 and grew through edition after edition until 1559. Geneva under his leadership became a refuge for Protestants fleeing persecution, and the academy he founded there in 1559 trained ministers who carried Reformed faith to France, Scotland, and the Netherlands.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His teaching on the greatness of God and the order of the Christian life shaped whole nations and churches, for both good and ill.

figures.name: Teresa of Avila
figures.summary: Teresa was a Spanish nun who, after years of feeling spiritually half-asleep, went through a deep awakening in midlife and set out to reform her order toward a simpler, more prayerful life. She founded new convents while battling illness, suspicion, and her own doubts, and she wrote about prayer with such warmth and plain good sense that her books are still read. She was practical and funny, once reportedly telling God, who could see how he treated his friends, that it was no wonder he had so few. Her grandfather was a Jewish convert who had been made to do public penance by the Inquisition, and she lived under its suspicion herself. With John of the Cross she founded a stricter branch of the Carmelites, and in The Interior Castle, written in 1577, she pictured the soul as a castle of many rooms with God dwelling at its center. In 1970 she became the first woman named a Doctor of the Church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She wrote about the inner life of prayer with rare clarity, and she proved that deep contemplation and hard practical work can belong to one person.

figures.name: Matteo Ricci
figures.summary: Ricci arrived in Macau in 1582 and spent years learning spoken and classical Chinese and studying the Confucian classics. He came to dress as a Chinese scholar, drew a map of the world for Chinese readers, translated Euclid's geometry with his friend and convert Xu Guangqi, and wrote a dialogue presenting Christian teaching in the language of Chinese philosophy. In 1601 he was allowed to live in Beijing, and when he died there in 1610 the emperor granted land for his burial. He permitted Chinese converts to keep honoring their ancestors, which he judged a civil rather than religious act. Rome later ruled against that approach, and the resulting controversy damaged the mission for a century.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He took another civilization's wisdom seriously enough to learn it from the inside, and the questions his work raised about how the gospel meets a culture are still open.

figures.name: Anne Hutchinson
figures.place: England, Massachusetts Bay, Rhode Island, and New Netherland
figures.summary: Anne Hutchinson was a midwife and mother of fifteen who followed her minister, John Cotton, from England to Boston. She began holding meetings in her home to discuss Sunday's sermons, and soon dozens of men and women were coming, while she criticized most of the colony's ministers for preaching a covenant of works. In 1637 the colony's leaders tried her. She defended herself so well that she nearly prevailed, until she claimed God had revealed things to her directly, which sealed her conviction. She was banished, excommunicated, and moved to Rhode Island and then to New Netherland, where she and most of her household were killed in 1643 during a war between the Dutch and the local Native people.
figures.whyTheyMatter: Her trial exposed how quickly a community founded for religious freedom could deny it to a woman who disagreed, and she remains a hard case on the limits of authority and conscience.

figures.name: Blaise Pascal
figures.summary: Pascal was a mathematical prodigy who built one of the first calculating machines, helped found the theory of probability, and conducted experiments on the vacuum. On the night of 23 November 1654 he had an overwhelming experience of God, and he wrote a short record of it that he sewed into his coat and carried until he died, naming the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob rather than the God of the philosophers. He defended the Jansenists of Port Royal in a set of satirical letters against the moral evasions of some Jesuit teachers. He died at thirty nine, leaving notes for a defense of Christianity that were published as the Pensées, including his famous wager and his portrait of human beings as both great and wretched.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He wrote for the skeptic as one of the sharpest minds of his century, and he insisted that the heart has reasons of its own without pretending reason did not matter.

figures.name: John Bunyan
figures.summary: Bunyan was a poor English tinker, a mender of pots, who came to a hard-won faith and began to preach without a license in a time when that was illegal. He spent twelve years in jail rather than promise to stop, and there he wrote, telling the story of a man named Christian walking from the City of Destruction to the Celestial City. That book, The Pilgrim's Progress, became one of the most widely read works in the English language. His spiritual autobiography, Grace Abounding to the Chief of Sinners, records years of torment over whether he had committed the unforgivable sin, and it is one of the most honest accounts of religious anxiety ever written.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He turned the Christian life into a story anyone could follow, and he showed that no formal education is needed to write something that lasts for centuries.

figures.name: Susanna Wesley
figures.role: Mother, teacher, and theologian of the household
figures.summary: Susanna was the youngest of many children of a Puritan minister in London, and she read theology from girlhood. She married the clergyman Samuel Wesley and bore nineteen children, many of whom died young, in a marriage strained by debt, a rectory fire, and her husband's time in debtors' prison. She schooled her children herself for six hours a day and met with each one privately every week to talk about their souls. When Samuel was away in London, she began reading sermons and praying with her household on Sunday evenings, the neighbors came until the kitchen held around two hundred, and when her husband objected she wrote back defending the meetings. Two of her sons, John and Charles, founded the Methodist movement.
figures.whyTheyMatter: Much of the method in Methodism was learned at her table, and she practiced a serious, ordered faith in the only pulpit her century allowed her.

figures.name: Jonathan Edwards
figures.summary: Edwards was a New England pastor and one of the sharpest minds America has produced, who saw a wave of revival sweep through his town of Northampton and across the colonies. He preached about the beauty and weight of God with a calm intensity, and in Religious Affections, published in 1746, he argued that true faith lives in the affections, the heart's settled inclinations toward God, and is not proven by the intensity of an experience. He owned enslaved people, a fact that sits in painful tension with his vision of God, and his own congregation dismissed him in 1750. He died in 1758, weeks after becoming president of the College of New Jersey, from a smallpox inoculation he took to encourage others.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He thought harder than almost anyone about the difference between true and false experiences of God, and his life holds together brilliance and serious moral failure.

figures.name: John Wesley
figures.summary: Wesley was an Anglican clergyman who, after years of religious effort, felt his heart strangely warmed at a meeting and finally trusted that Christ had saved even him. He then spent decades riding tens of thousands of miles on horseback to preach in fields and streets to people the established church ignored, especially the poor and the working class. He organized his converts into small groups for prayer and accountability, and out of his work the Methodist movement was born. The moment of the warmed heart came at a meeting on Aldersgate Street in London on 24 May 1738. He remained a priest of the Church of England all his life. In 1774 he published Thoughts upon Slavery, an attack on slavery and the trade that fed it, and one of the last letters he wrote, in 1791, urged Wilberforce to keep fighting it.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He carried the gospel to people the church had overlooked and built a way of organizing ordinary believers for growth and care that spread around the world.

figures.name: Absalom Jones
figures.role: Priest and founder of St. Thomas African Episcopal Church
figures.summary: Absalom Jones was born enslaved in Delaware and taught himself to read from whatever he could find. In Philadelphia he worked for years to buy his wife's freedom first, so their children would be born free, and then his own. With Richard Allen he founded the Free African Society in 1787 and helped lead Black Philadelphians through the yellow fever epidemic of 1793. In 1794 he opened the African Episcopal Church of St. Thomas, and in 1804 he became the first Black priest in the Episcopal Church. On the first day of 1808, when the American ban on importing enslaved people took effect, he preached a sermon of thanksgiving that also called for the end of slavery itself.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He built a church for people the white church would not seat as equals, and he did it patiently, from inside a tradition that did not yet treat him as an equal.

figures.name: William Wilberforce
figures.place: Hull, London, and Clapham in England
figures.summary: Wilberforce entered Parliament at twenty one as a witty, ambitious young man and underwent an evangelical conversion in his mid twenties. He thought about leaving politics for the ministry, and the old slave ship captain turned pastor John Newton counseled him to stay. In 1787 he wrote in his journal that God had set before him two great objects, the suppression of the slave trade and the reformation of the nation's morals. He brought abolition before Parliament again and again and saw it defeated or stalled for nearly twenty years before the trade was outlawed in 1807. He worked alongside a circle of evangelical friends at Clapham and in partnership with Quakers and Black abolitionists. He also supported harsh measures against political dissent at home, which his admirers do not always mention. He died in 1833, days after hearing that the bill to abolish slavery itself would pass.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He shows what persistence in public life looks like when faith is the reason for it, and he shows that even a reformer can be blind in other directions.

figures.name: Richard Allen
figures.role: Preacher and first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church
figures.summary: Richard Allen was born enslaved, came to faith under Methodist preaching as a teenager, and later bought his freedom. He preached across the middle states and settled in Philadelphia, where he and Absalom Jones founded the Free African Society in 1787. When Black worshipers were pulled from their knees at St. George's Methodist Church, they walked out, and Allen went on to dedicate Bethel church in 1794 in a converted blacksmith shop. For years white Methodist leaders tried to control the congregation and its property, and Allen fought them through the courts until Bethel won. In 1816 he and other Black Methodist leaders formed the African Methodist Episcopal Church, and he was consecrated its first bishop. He also opened his church to the Underground Railroad and opposed schemes to send free Black Americans to Africa.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He built one of the first independent Black denominations in America and proved that Black Christians did not need white permission to be the church.

figures.name: William Carey
figures.summary: Carey was an English shoemaker with little schooling who taught himself languages and became convinced that Christians had a duty to carry the gospel to the whole world. He sailed to India in 1793 and spent the rest of his life there. With his colleagues at Serampore, a Danish settlement near Calcutta, he oversaw translations of the Scriptures into dozens of Indian languages and dialects, started schools and Serampore College, and campaigned against the burning of widows. He buried a child and watched his wife lose her mind under the strain, and he kept working.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He helped launch the modern missionary movement, and his motto, to expect great things from God and attempt great things for God, still stirs people to action.

figures.name: Sojourner Truth
figures.place: Ulster County in New York, then across the northern states
figures.summary: She was born Isabella, enslaved in a Dutch speaking household in New York, and was sold several times as a child. In 1826 she walked away to freedom carrying her infant daughter, and soon after she went to court to recover her young son, who had been illegally sold into Alabama, and won, one of the first Black women to win such a case against a white man. A conversion experience gave her an intense, lifelong sense of Jesus as her friend. In 1843 she took the name Sojourner Truth and set out to preach, and she became one of the most powerful speakers in the abolitionist and women's rights movements. The most famous version of her Akron speech of 1851 was written down years later by someone else in a dialect she did not speak; the earliest report is plainer and just as strong. She met President Lincoln in 1864 and worked for freedpeople after the war.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She preached with a moral authority no one had given her, and her life insists that the gospel and human dignity cannot be pulled apart.

figures.name: Phoebe Palmer
figures.summary: Phoebe Palmer was a Methodist laywoman in New York whose faith was forged in grief; she lost three of her children in infancy. From her home she led the Tuesday Meeting for the Promotion of Holiness, a weekly gathering begun by her sister that drew bishops and professors along with ordinary believers. She taught that a Christian could lay everything on the altar, trust God's promise, and receive a clean heart, and her book The Way of Holiness spread that teaching widely. She spent years preaching in revivals in North America and Britain, helped begin a mission in the Five Points slum of New York, and wrote The Promise of the Father, a defense of women's preaching from the day of Pentecost.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She helped launch the holiness movement that later fed Pentecostalism, and she defended the right of women to speak what God had given them.

figures.name: Samuel Ajayi Crowther
figures.place: Yorubaland, Sierra Leone, and the Niger
figures.summary: Ajayi was a Yoruba boy of about twelve when slave raiders captured him in 1821. He was sold to Portuguese traders, but the ship was stopped by a British naval patrol and he was landed in Sierra Leone, where he became a Christian and took the name Samuel Crowther. He was the first student at Fourah Bay College, joined an expedition up the Niger, and was ordained in England. He translated the Bible into Yoruba and wrote grammars and vocabularies of several West African languages. In 1846 he found his mother, from whom he had been torn as a boy, and she was later baptized. In 1864 he was consecrated in Canterbury Cathedral as the first African Anglican bishop of modern times. In his last years younger European missionaries undermined his authority and suspended his clergy, and after his death he was replaced by a European.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He showed what an African church led by Africans could be, and the way he was pushed aside shows how the missionary movement could betray its own best convictions.

figures.name: Søren Kierkegaard
figures.summary: Kierkegaard was the brooding son of a wealthy, guilt haunted father in Copenhagen. He broke off his engagement to Regine Olsen, the love of his life, believing he could not give her a true marriage, and then poured out a stream of books, many under invented names, including Either/Or and Fear and Trembling in 1843. He argued that faith is not a conclusion reached by reasoning or a membership inherited at birth but a personal decision before God, made in fear and trembling. Under his own name he wrote Works of Love, a long meditation on the command to love one's neighbor. In his last year he attacked the Danish state church in a series of pamphlets, arguing that a Christianity everyone belonged to by birth had quietly abolished the Christianity of the New Testament. He collapsed in the street in 1855 and died weeks later.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He named the problem of a comfortable Christendom more sharply than anyone, and his questions matter most in a culture where faith is assumed and seldom followed.

figures.name: Frederick Douglass
figures.place: Maryland, then Massachusetts, Rochester, and Washington
figures.summary: Douglass was born enslaved in Maryland and learned to read as a boy, first from his mistress until her husband forbade it, and then in secret. He came to faith as a teenager, and he later remembered teaching other enslaved people to read the Bible until a mob that included church members broke up the school. He escaped in 1838, became a licensed preacher in an African Methodist Episcopal Zion congregation in New Bedford, and then one of the greatest orators in American history. His Narrative of 1845 ended with an appendix distinguishing the Christianity of Christ, which he loved, from the slaveholding religion of America, which he called corrupt and hypocritical. In 1852 he asked what the Fourth of July could mean to the enslaved.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He gave the American church a verdict it has never fully answered, and he gave it as a man who still believed in the Christ that church had betrayed.

figures.name: Harriet Tubman
figures.place: Dorchester County in Maryland, then Philadelphia and Auburn, New York
figures.summary: She was born Araminta Ross, enslaved in Maryland, and as a teenager was struck in the head by a heavy weight thrown at another slave, an injury that left her with seizures and vivid dreams for the rest of her life. She understood those dreams and her constant prayer as God's guidance. She escaped in 1849 and then went back into Maryland about thirteen times, leading around seventy people to freedom, including members of her own family, and never losing one. During the Civil War she served the Union army as a scout, spy, and nurse, and in 1863 she helped lead the raid on the Combahee River that freed more than seven hundred people. She spent her old age in Auburn, New York, caring for the elderly and poor through her church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She trusted God with her life again and again for the sake of others, and her faith was never separate from the work of setting captives free.

figures.name: Charles Spurgeon
figures.summary: Spurgeon was preaching to thousands in London while still in his early twenties, drawing crowds so large that a great hall was built to hold them. His sermons were warm, plain, and full of Christ, and they were printed and read around the world week by week. He struggled for years with crippling depression and chronic illness, and he spoke about that darkness openly, which has comforted many who carry the same weight. He never attended university or seminary, and he founded a college to train pastors who, like him, lacked formal education. In his last years he withdrew from the Baptist Union in what was called the Downgrade Controversy, warning that the churches were quietly surrendering the authority of Scripture.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He showed that the deepest preaching can also be the plainest, and his honesty about depression speaks to believers who suffer in silence.

figures.name: Amanda Berry Smith
figures.place: Maryland, New York, England, India, and Liberia
figures.summary: Amanda Berry was born enslaved in Maryland, and her father bought the family's freedom. She worked for years as a washerwoman and cook, buried most of her children and two husbands, and in 1868 experienced what the holiness movement called entire sanctification. She began singing and preaching at camp meetings, often to largely white crowds who had come to see a Black woman preach and stayed to be moved. In 1878 she sailed for England, then spent time in India, then about eight years in Liberia, working without the backing of a mission board. She was never ordained by her own church. Back in America she published her autobiography and opened a home for Black orphans near Chicago.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She preached across three continents with no office and no sponsor, and her life shows how much of the church's mission was carried by people its structures did not recognize.

figures.name: Lottie Moon
figures.place: Virginia, then Shandong province in China
figures.summary: Charlotte Digges Moon was one of the most highly educated women in the American South of her day, fluent in several languages. In 1873 she sailed for China to join her sister as a missionary and spent almost forty years there, first teaching girls and then moving into villages of the interior to evangelize, dressing as the local people did. She wrote frank letters home urging Southern Baptist women to organize and give, and in 1888 they formed a missionary union and took up a Christmas offering, which was later named for her. During years of famine she gave away her own food and money, and she died in 1912 aboard a ship in the harbor at Kobe, badly malnourished, on the way home.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She gave her whole life, and in the end her body, to a people far from home, and she pushed her own church to take women's work seriously.

figures.name: Pandita Ramabai
figures.summary: Ramabai was born into a Brahmin family and taught Sanskrit by her father, unusual for a girl. Her parents died in a famine, and she and her brother wandered across India reciting the sacred texts, until the scholars of Calcutta honored her learning with the titles Pandita and Sarasvati. She married outside her caste and was widowed with a baby daughter after less than two years. In England she became a Christian and, in America, raised support for her work. In 1889 she opened a home and school for child widows, and later, at Mukti near Pune, took in hundreds of women and girls rescued from famine. A revival broke out at Mukti in 1905. She spent her last years translating the Bible into Marathi from the Hebrew and Greek, and she remained both a devoted Christian and an Indian who resisted being made into a Western one.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She fought for the women her society discarded, and she insisted that an Indian could follow Christ without abandoning India.

figures.name: William Wadé Harris
figures.place: Liberia, the Ivory Coast, and the Gold Coast
figures.summary: Harris was a Grebo man from Liberia, educated in mission schools, who worked as a teacher and became involved in politics. While imprisoned in 1910 he had a vision he understood as a call from the angel Gabriel to be a prophet. In 1913 he set out walking east along the coast of the Ivory Coast and into the Gold Coast in a white robe, carrying a cross, a Bible, and a calabash. He called people to burn their charms, worship the one God, keep the Lord's day, and wait for teachers who would bring the Bible, and huge numbers were baptized before French colonial authorities expelled him. When Methodist missionaries arrived years later, they found thousands of believers waiting for them with Bibles they could not yet read.
figures.whyTheyMatter: In about eighteen months he baptized more people in the Ivory Coast than its missions had in decades, and he did it as an African prophet speaking to Africans.

figures.name: Tikhon of Moscow
figures.summary: Vasily Bellavin became the monk Tikhon and served for several years as the Orthodox bishop in North America, where he helped organize a scattered church of immigrants. In November 1917, as the Bolsheviks took power, a church council restored the office of patriarch of Moscow, abolished for two centuries, and Tikhon was chosen by lot. Within months he condemned the violence of the new regime. As the state seized church property and killed clergy, he was arrested and pressured, and he tried to protect his people without surrendering the church to the state. He died in 1925 under surveillance, and the Russian church later numbered him among its saints.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He led a church into the first great modern persecution and showed what faithfulness looks like when there is no good option left.

figures.name: Amy Carmichael
figures.place: Northern Ireland, then Dohnavur in South India
figures.summary: Amy Carmichael grew up in a Presbyterian family in Northern Ireland and began her work among the mill girls of Belfast. After a brief time in Japan, she went to South India in 1895, adopted Indian dress, and traveled with a band of Indian Christian women evangelists. In 1901 a young girl who had escaped from a Hindu temple where she had been dedicated to service came to her, and from then on Carmichael took in children at risk of temple prostitution. The community at Dohnavur grew to hundreds of children, run as a family rather than an institution. A fall in 1931 left her largely bedridden for the last twenty years of her life, during which she wrote many of the books for which she is known.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She gave her life to rescuing children the world did not count, and she kept writing about the cost of love from a sickbed.

figures.name: William J. Seymour
figures.role: Pastor of the Azusa Street Mission
figures.summary: Seymour was the son of formerly enslaved parents in Louisiana and lost the sight of one eye to smallpox. In Houston he studied under the white holiness teacher Charles Parham, but segregation meant he had to listen to the lessons from the hallway. Invited to preach in Los Angeles in 1906, he was locked out of the church that had called him, and he began a prayer meeting in a home that moved to a former church building on Azusa Street. For about three years the mission drew people of every race and many nations, who prayed, sang, and spoke in tongues together, and missionaries went out from it around the world. Parham later denounced the racial mixing, and much of the movement split along the color line. Seymour died in 1922, still pastoring a small congregation there.
figures.whyTheyMatter: A Black preacher led the revival from which one of the largest Christian movements in the world grew, and its early refusal of the color line is a judgment on what came after.

figures.name: Karl Barth
figures.summary: Barth was a young Swiss pastor in the industrial village of Safenwil, working alongside laborers for fair wages, when the First World War began and he saw his revered German teachers publicly support it. He concluded that the liberal theology they had taught him, which tied God closely to human culture and progress, had failed. His commentary on Romans, first published in 1919, insisted that God is God and not a projection of our religion, and it made him famous. As a professor in Germany he became the main author of the Barmen Declaration of 1934 and was forced out for refusing to swear unconditional loyalty to Hitler. From Basel he wrote the Church Dogmatics, a vast, unfinished work centered on God's self revelation in Jesus Christ. For more than three decades Charlotte von Kirschbaum, his assistant and close collaborator on the Dogmatics, lived in his household, an arrangement that caused his wife, Nelly, deep and lasting pain, and that his own letters and his biographers do not hide.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He called the church back to the Word of God when it was bowing to the spirit of the age, and he did so at the moment the cost was highest.

figures.name: Sadhu Sundar Singh
figures.summary: Sundar Singh grew up in a devout Sikh family in the Punjab. After his mother died when he was fourteen, he grew bitter, publicly burned a Bible, and resolved to take his own life if God did not reveal himself; that night, he said, he saw Jesus. His family disowned him, and after his baptism he took up the saffron robe of an Indian holy man and walked the roads of India and into Tibet, preaching Christ in a form Indians could recognize. He liked to say that India needed the water of life in an Indian cup. In the 1920s he traveled to Europe and elsewhere and drew large crowds. In 1929 he set out for Tibet again and was never seen again.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He showed that following Christ did not require becoming Western, and his life gave Indian Christians a way of discipleship that was their own.

figures.name: Mother Maria Skobtsova
figures.summary: She was born Elizaveta Pilenko, a poet in the intellectual circles of St. Petersburg and a revolutionary who briefly served as mayor of a southern Russian town during the civil war. In exile in Paris, after the death of her young daughter, she became an Orthodox nun in 1932, but an unusual one, who turned a rented house into a shelter and kitchen for the poor and the displaced. When the Nazis occupied Paris, her house hid Jews, and her chaplain issued them baptismal certificates to help them escape. She was arrested in 1943 and died at Ravensbrück on 31 March 1945, weeks before the war ended. Her son died in another camp. Accounts from survivors say she may have taken another woman's place, and in 2004 the Patriarchate of Constantinople recognized her as a saint.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She believed the neighbor is an icon of God, and she treated the hunted of Paris as if Christ had come to her door.

figures.name: Corrie ten Boom
figures.summary: Corrie ten Boom was an unmarried watchmaker in her father's shop in Haarlem, the first woman licensed as a watchmaker in the Netherlands. During the German occupation the family's house became a refuge, with a hidden room built behind a false wall, for Jews and resistance workers. In February 1944 they were betrayed and arrested. Her father died in prison ten days later, and her sister Betsie died at Ravensbrück, where she had kept telling Corrie that no pit was so deep that God was not deeper still. Corrie was released in late 1944. After the war she spoke in more than sixty countries, and she told of meeting a former Ravensbrück guard who asked her forgiveness, and of how she could not give it until she asked God for the power to take his hand. Her book The Hiding Place appeared in 1971.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She told the truth about how hard forgiveness is, which is why her testimony to it can be believed.

figures.name: C.S. Lewis
figures.summary: Lewis was an Oxford literature professor and a confirmed atheist who, after long arguments with friends and a slow change of mind, came to faith in his thirties. He went on to write some of the most beloved Christian books of the past century, from plainspoken defenses of the faith to the Narnia stories read by children and adults alike. He wrote with humor and imagination, and after the death of his wife he wrote with raw honesty about grief and doubt. His BBC radio talks during the Second World War became Mere Christianity. His conversion owed much to a long night's conversation in 1931 with J. R. R. Tolkien and Hugo Dyson about myth and the gospel. His wife was Joy Davidman, and A Grief Observed, his record of mourning her, first appeared under a pseudonym.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He helped countless skeptics take Christianity seriously by speaking their language, and he never pretended that faith means the end of hard questions.

figures.name: Howard Thurman
figures.place: Daytona Beach, Atlanta, San Francisco, and Boston
figures.summary: Thurman was raised in Florida largely by his grandmother, who had been enslaved. She had him read the Bible aloud to her but refused to hear most of Paul's letters, because the white preachers of her youth had used them to tell slaves to obey their masters. That memory shaped his life's question: what does the religion of Jesus say to people with their backs against the wall. In 1936 he led a delegation to India and met Gandhi. In 1944 he helped found the Church for the Fellowship of All Peoples in San Francisco, one of the first intentionally interracial congregations in the country, and in 1949 he published Jesus and the Disinherited, which Martin Luther King Jr. is said to have carried with him. He became dean of the chapel at Boston University in 1953.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He found in Jesus, a poor Jew under Roman occupation, the resources for the dispossessed to refuse both fear and hatred.

figures.name: John Sung
figures.place: Fujian in China, the United States, and Southeast Asia
figures.summary: Song Shangjie was the son of a Methodist pastor in southern China. He went to America, earned a doctorate in chemistry at Ohio State University, and then enrolled at Union Theological Seminary in New York, where the liberal teaching left him in spiritual crisis. After a dramatic conversion experience, the seminary had him committed to a psychiatric hospital, where he spent about six months reading the Bible through again and again. He returned to China in 1927 and became the most powerful evangelist of his generation, preaching across China and Southeast Asia with fierce intensity, calling for repentance and forming preaching bands of ordinary believers. Illness ended his ministry, and he died in 1944 at forty two.
figures.whyTheyMatter: His preaching prepared a generation of Chinese Christians for the persecution to come, and he showed that revival in Asia would be led by Asians.

figures.name: Watchman Nee
figures.summary: Ni Tuosheng, known in English as Watchman Nee, came to faith as a student in 1920 and was shaped by the British missionary Margaret Barber. He came to believe the Chinese church should not depend on foreign denominations, and he founded local assemblies, one church in each city, led by Chinese believers. His teaching on the Christian life, later published in English as The Normal Christian Life, was read around the world. He also ran a pharmaceutical business to support his co workers, which the Communist state later used against him. Arrested in 1952, he was tried and sentenced to fifteen years, was kept in prison past his term, and died in a labor camp in 1972.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He built a church that could survive without the West, and then he suffered for it for twenty years.

figures.name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
figures.summary: Bonhoeffer was a young German pastor and scholar who refused to go along with Hitler and the part of the church that bowed to him. He helped lead a resistant church, ran an underground seminary, and wrote about the cost of following Jesus rather than the cheap comfort of an easy faith. Drawn into a plot against Hitler, he was arrested, imprisoned, and hanged days before the camp was liberated. His Discipleship, published in 1937, opened with the difference between cheap grace and costly grace, and Life Together came out of the shared life at his underground seminary at Finkenwalde. In 1939 he sailed to safety in New York and returned within weeks, convinced he could have no part in rebuilding Germany after the war if he did not share its trials with his people. He was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He named the difference between cheap grace and costly grace, and he paid for his convictions with his life when most around him stayed silent.

figures.name: Fannie Lou Hamer
figures.summary: Fannie Lou Hamer was the youngest of twenty children in a sharecropping family and began picking cotton at six. In 1961 a white doctor sterilized her without her consent during another surgery. In 1962 she tried to register to vote and was fired and evicted the same day. In 1963, returning from a voter training workshop, she was arrested in Winona, Mississippi, and beaten in the jail so badly that she carried the injuries the rest of her life. In 1964 she testified before the Democratic National Convention's credentials committee for the Mississippi Freedom Democratic Party, and her account was carried on national television. She led singing at mass meetings, especially This Little Light of Mine, and her speeches were full of Scripture. Later she founded a farm cooperative to feed poor families in the Delta.
figures.whyTheyMatter: She showed that the freedom movement was carried by ordinary church people, and she refused to let America look away from what was being done in the name of order.

figures.name: Óscar Romero
figures.summary: Romero was known as a bookish, cautious priest, and when he was made archbishop of San Salvador in 1977, the powerful expected him to keep the church quiet. Weeks later his friend Rutilio Grande, a Jesuit who worked among poor farmworkers, was murdered, and Romero changed. In weekly sermons broadcast by radio across the country, he named the disappeared and the dead and demanded justice. On 23 March 1980 he appealed directly to soldiers to obey God rather than orders to kill their own people. The next day he was shot while celebrating Mass in a hospital chapel. A United Nations commission later found that his killing was ordered by a leader of the death squads. In 2018 the Catholic Church declared him a saint.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He was converted by the suffering of his people, and he shows that a shepherd's first duty is to the sheep and not to the powerful.

figures.name: Festo Kivengere
figures.summary: Kivengere grew up in Uganda and was converted in 1941 through the East African Revival, whose people confessed sin openly and crossed tribal lines to seek reconciliation. He became a teacher, then an evangelist who preached across Africa and the world, and in 1972 bishop of Kigezi. When Idi Amin's regime murdered Archbishop Janani Luwum in 1977, Kivengere was also in danger and fled the country. Within months he published a small book titled I Love Idi Amin, arguing that the cross required him to forgive even the man who had killed his friends. He returned home after Amin's fall.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He practiced forgiveness in the face of a murderous regime without calling evil anything other than evil.

figures.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
figures.summary: King was the son and grandson of Baptist preachers in Atlanta, trained at Morehouse College, Crozer Theological Seminary, and Boston University, and became pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery in 1954. The next year he was chosen to lead the Montgomery bus boycott, and he spent the rest of his life leading a movement of nonviolent resistance rooted in the Black church. In April 1963, jailed in Birmingham, he answered eight white clergymen who had called the protests unwise and untimely, writing that he was most disappointed not by open racists but by white moderates who preferred order to justice, and that the church had become a thermometer recording the temperature of society rather than a thermostat changing it. The FBI spied on him and harassed him for years. Scholars editing his papers later found that he had copied passages in his graduate work without credit, a real failing, named honestly, that sits beside what he gave the church rather than erasing it. He was killed in Memphis in 1968, supporting striking sanitation workers.
figures.whyTheyMatter: He called the American church to live what it preached, and his letter from a jail cell remains a searching word to comfortable Christians.

figures.name: René Padilla and Samuel Escobar
figures.place: Ecuador, Argentina, Peru, and across Latin America
figures.summary: René Padilla, born in Ecuador, and Samuel Escobar, born in Peru, worked for years among university students in Latin America, where they saw evangelical faith often arriving tied to North American culture and silent about poverty and injustice. With others they founded the Latin American Theological Fraternity in 1970. At the Lausanne Congress on World Evangelization in 1974, both gave addresses that challenged the gathering to reject a gospel shaped by American culture and consumer society and to recover the whole biblical mission, word and deed together. Their work helped shape the Lausanne Covenant's statement that social responsibility is part of Christian duty, and the idea they called integral mission spread across the global church.
figures.whyTheyMatter: They taught the evangelical world that the gospel of the kingdom concerns the whole of life, and that the churches of the Global South have theology to teach, not only to receive.
